What I Do

I focus on the details that make a Roblox game feel like an actual world instead of a collection of systems.

NPCs with a reason to existCharacters get a role, visual identity, personality and something useful for the player to interact with.
Quests with varietyI use gathering, services, exploration, choices, repairs and other objectives so players are not always fighting the same enemy.
Dialogue that feels aliveI write around the character and gameplay, so the player knows what to do without every NPC sounding the same.

QUEST DESIGN

Quests That Aren't Just Bandit Beaters

I help with quests by making them diverse. Players should be able to repair something, gather a rare item, explore, help an NPC or discover something weird — not just defeat another group of enemies.

ObjectivesRewardsVarietyWorldbuilding

DIALOGUE

NPC Dialogue & Interactions

I write dialogue that gives NPCs a clear personality while still making their gameplay purpose easy to understand.

PersonalityChoicesPlayer Flow

Mechanic — Gunman Repair

“Hold it. That's a Gunman you've got there... Looks like it's seen better days.”

“I can repair damaged Gunmen and get them back into fighting condition.”

“It'll cost you 1 Gold Coin. Fair price for honest work.”

“So, what'll it be?”

Accept: “Stand back. This won't take long.”

Not enough Gold: “Looks like you're short on Gold Coins. Come back when you can afford the repair.”

Already repaired: “There's nothing wrong with this one. Save your Gold Coin for when it's actually damaged.”

Leave: “No worries. I'll be here if your Gunman ever needs fixing.”

Barber

“Welcome in. Need a fresh look?”

“A good haircut can change how people see you. Pick a style and I'll take care of the rest.”

Player: “I want a haircut.”

Price: 5 Gold Coins. If the player has enough: “Perfect. Sit down and let me work my magic.” / “All done. Looking sharp!”

Not enough: “Sorry, but a good haircut isn't free.”

Weapon Dealer

“Need something to defend yourself? You've come to the right place.”

“I sell reliable weapons. Nothing fancy, just gear that gets the job done.”

Show weapons: “Take your pick. Treat them well and they'll last.”

Who are you? “I'm just someone who knows weapons. In a world full of battles, it's better to be prepared than empty-handed.”

Traveler #2

“So basically, I'm looking for a rare rock inside a giant pile of rocks.”

“Exactly.”

“And what do I get for doing all this?”

“If I told you, it wouldn't be a surprise.”

That kind of back-and-forth is what I like using to make a quest feel like it belongs to a character, instead of reading like a checklist.

PROJECT MANAGEMENT

Keeping Development Organized

I break bigger ideas into tasks, keep priorities clear, document important details and help connect design with the people building the feature.

RoadmapsTask PlanningDocumentationTesting

I start by making sure everyone knows what the feature is supposed to do. Then I split it into smaller pieces so programmers, builders, artists and testers can work without guessing what the design means.

I also like testing early. If a quest feels repetitive, an NPC is confusing, or a reward does not feel worth getting, it is better to fix that while the feature is still being built.

My goal is simple: clearer tasks, less confusion and a game that keeps moving forward.

How I Work

I keep the design practical. The point is to make ideas clear enough that a team can actually build them.

01

Start with the player

I decide what the player is doing, why they would care, and what makes the interaction different from the last one.

02

Build the character and objective

I give the NPC a role, personality and dialogue, then connect that to an objective and reward that make sense.

03

Write it clearly

I turn the idea into dialogue, objectives, conditions and reward text so the rest of the team can understand it without guessing.

04

Test and make it less boring

I look for repetitive objectives, confusing instructions and moments where the player has no reason to care, then improve them.
